Less is known about how life history traits interact\\nwith stochasticity and population structure of finite populations to\\npredict near-term extinction risk. Through empirically parameterized\\nmatrix population models, we study the impact of life history\\n(reproduction, pace), stochasticity (environmental, demographic), and\\npopulation history (existing, novel) on the near-term population\\ndynamics of finite populations of plant species. Among fast and slow\\npace and either uniform or increasing reproductive intensity or short or\\nlong reproductive stage duration, slow, semelparous species are at the\\ngreatest risk of extinction. Long reproductive stages buffer existing\\npopulations from extinction while extinction risk of novel populations\\ndecrease when reproductive effort is uniformly spread across the\\nreproductive stage. Our study highlights the importance of population\\nstructure, pace, and two distinct aspects of parity for predicting\\nnear-term extinction risk.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.22541/au.168813053.31155982/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2023, 6, 30]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.5211739\", \"title\": [\"The Self-Body Boundary and Preliminary Verification of Agi Systems: A Theoretical Integration Framework Informed by Internal and External Sensations\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5211739\"…
